items.body: ACTORS Our Love Will Live Forever Artoffact Records There’s been a real sense of inevitability to the rise of Vancouver post-punk quartet ACTORS since the release of 2018’s debut LP It Will Come to You. Vocalist, guitarist, producer and bandleader Jason Corbett’s vision for melodic post-punk as an amalgamation of hooks, atmosphere and sharp production has always been an easy sell (as evidenced by their incredibly loyal international fanbase), but in a world where the best execution is no guarantee of success, ACTORS have never seemed like they were going anywhere but up. New album Our Love Will Last Forever feels no different in that regard, its studied mix of danceable rhythms and memorable choruses adding to their momentum. On its surface, the appeal of the record is extremely obvious: the songs are good. Really good. There’s a warmth and familiarity to cuts like “Youth” that comes through in Corbett’s vocals, the incredibly tight rhythm section of drummer Adam Fink and bassist Kendall Wooding, and the backing vocals and keys of Shannon Hemmett. It all feels natural, easy, fun to move to. That sensibility ports handily into the restrained but ever building sound of “Object of Desire”, whose twinned vocals are saturated and compressed together, adding to the effect when each voice breaks out on its own during the underplayed, yet somehow still massive chorus. The quietly stunning “In Real Life” stands as a testament to ACTORS’ songcraft, its relative simplicity belying how deeply it sinks its claws in, brimming with a melancholia so thick it’s intoxicating. It’s almost certainly the best song ACTORS have ever released, and not for any reason beyond how relatable its plaintive hope comes across. Beyond the actual songwriting and performances, Our Love Will Live Forever is a document of Corbett’s skill as a producer, and his understanding of what makes his own songs tick. The mix is thick and lively, and while there’s always have plenty going on, the LP never feel overly busy. Listen to how CTRL keeps the bass way up in front, backing it with synths and a disco drumbeat that provides room for vocal ad libs, quick guitar licks, bursts of keys, and swells of delay and reverb that serve the cut instead of detracting from it. That refined approach is a big key to making it work; the funky cowbell and claps that put the Devo-esque new wave boogie of “Stimulation” over the top could have been tacky, but the track’s arrangement and mix keep them tasteful. It really is a tremendous sounding record from a production standpoint both clever when suitable (listen to how the wink and a smile of “Bad Boys (Don’t Go to Heaven)” jumps from dry and zoomed in to lush and widescreen in the blink of an eye), but always with the best interests of the song in mind; when it’s time to let things breathe, as on “Dead Inside”, the song is presented simply, as it might sound coming off a stage rather than from a meticulous multi-tracked recording. Of all of the record’s merits, Our Love Will Live Forever‘s greatest strength lies in taking ACTORS already well-established sound to new levels. The bass rumbles harder, the grooves are tighter, the melodies more instantaneous. For the relatively simple remit of zeroing in on what works and doing more of it, it ends up being quite an achievement, and what’s more, one that somehow sounds effortless. Recommended. Buy it. items._cn_summary: ACTORS 来自加拿大温哥华，这张专辑延续了 2018 年首作以来的旋律化后朋克路线，将抓人的钩子、氛围化的音色与锐利的制作融为一体。主唱兼制作人 Jason Corbett 在录音室层面的把控尤为突出——混音饱满而鲜活，贝斯始终前置于前景，合成器、迪斯科鼓点与人声即兴穿插其间，延迟与混响服务于歌曲本身而非堆砌炫技。歌曲如《Youth》温暖易记，《Object of Desire》以压缩叠合的双人声制造张力，《In Real Life》以极简编曲承载浓烈忧郁，被视为乐队迄今最佳单曲。制作细节方面，《Stimulation》中的牛铃与拍手在 Devo 式新浪潮律动中保持克制品味，《Bad Boys》从干声窄景瞬间切换到宽阔声场，体现了对歌曲结构的精准理解。整体而言，这是一张制作精良、旋律突出、节奏鲜明的后朋克专辑，适合暗潮与新浪潮爱好者。

items._cn_summary: Ezra Collective 第五张专辑呈现一段跨越非洲节奏、雷鬼与嘻哈元素的爵士旅程。作品以深沉的律动骨架支撑，将五种文化语境编织为统一的听觉叙事。客座音乐人的参与并未分散核心五人组的群体能量，反而丰富了整体的对话层次。社区意识、精神性与集体动力构成作品的根基，这些抽象理念通过紧凑的器乐编排转化为可感的音乐语言。专辑跨越国界与流派边界的姿态贯穿始终，每首曲目都在爵士框架内融入世界音乐的色彩与嘻哈的节奏逻辑。整体而言，这是一张注重群组协作与文化交融的当代爵士作品，在传统与现代、非洲根源与英国城市语境之间找到了平衡点。

Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: Camilla Hole Trio 在新专辑中延续了上一张作品中对外拓展的思路，从挪威西部民间舞曲 Springleik 取材，高音萨克斯主奏旋律，低音提琴与鼓提供节奏支撑，随后模合成器与颤音琴以叠录方式加入。三位乐手不拘泥于固定角色，旋律在萨克斯与贝斯之间交接，节奏层逐步打开，作品从主题陈述滑入自由即兴段落，结尾又回归原始旋律。上一张专辑曾将科幻合成器音色与挪威传统素材并置，本次则更加落地，但探索本国以外民间音乐语汇的方向未变。专辑呈现了北欧爵士与传统素材在即兴框架下的对话，结构松散而层次丰富。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.excerpt: An acoustic guitar can make a room feel inhabited; on Dizzy Scent’s Doggy’s Cake, it also makes you wonder what else might be in there. items.body: An acoustic guitar can make a room feel inhabited; on Dizzy Scent’s Doggy’s Cake, it also makes you wonder what else might be in there. Fingers travel audibly across strings, gentle strumming takes on the unease of branches brushing a house after dark, and a voice slips between a confidential murmur and a disorienting chorus. Across these six songs, familiar folk gestures acquire strange proportions, with tenderness, sensuality, and distress sharing the same small space. Released on September 11, 2026, Doggy’s Cake follows July’s debut album, My Polarizing Nature, from independent singer, songwriter, and guitarist Dizzy Scent. She describes her approach as “dark raw,” pursuing instinctive playing and unusual chords while managing her career herself. In her account of the EP’s creation, depression, occult interests, and frustration with the music industry all feed into the work. Her attachment to imperfection comes with a pointed explanation: “Imperfection has a greater impact on humans because, with perfection, we already know what to expect.” That philosophy suits a record in which the movement of a hand across strings and an unguarded vocal sound carry so much feeling. The relationship between guitar and singer stays exposed, allowing changes in delivery to alter the character of an entire passage. The EP’s first track, “Witch (When Im Completely Red)” opens with acoustic strumming that scratches like the branches of a skeletal old tree against the side of a house at night. Over that dry contact, her soft, ghostly vocals develop a folky flutter, then climb into high notes resembling wind whistling around the building. There is something eerie and otherworldly about the way those two elements occupy the same space: the guitar feels close and physical, while the singing seems to drift beyond its reach. At nearly seven minutes, the opener gives that sensation ample time to develop. Dizzy’s release notes connect the song to her fascination with magic and admiration for Papus, placing its supernatural associations within her broader occult interests. The gently strummed opening of “My Dark Sides” has the plain, soothing shape of a lullaby. Her voice enters in a hushed whisper, suggesting an incantation murmured quietly enough to be mistaken for someone talking to herself. As the singing quivers and flutters, higher notes take on the character of a cry carried by the wind. The effect suggests glimpses of an inner world projected into the room, with the simplicity of the guitar making every vocal tremor more conspicuous. Dizzy describes the song as an effort to free herself from fears and the darker aspects of her character; the tentative intimacy of the performance gives those concerns a fragile, immediate presence. “Unchangeable” pushes the guitar forward with deep, resonant tones, its volume drawing attention to the sound of fingers gliding along the strings. Her singing carries a smoldering sensuality, almost jazzy in character, while retaining its folky appeal. A dreamy, ethereal quality surrounds that tactile opening. Halfway through, the arrangement becomes pleasingly unruly, resembling a chorus of ghostly voices, and her singing climbs higher while preserving its silky texture. The shortest song on the EP packs considerable movement into its two and a half minutes. According to Dizzy, it grew from months of searching for recognition and fielding opinions about her music before finding someone who acknowledged its value. She remains attached to the unusual chords and imperfections that make the work hers. Soft guitar strumming moves through “So That Means To Be An Artist And Sing ?” like footsteps on a moonlit walk. Dizzy’s languid, smoky delivery recalls PJ Harvey, its sensuality carried by the ease with which her voice drifts into the song. Around the one-minute mark, the arrangement and layered vocals become ghostly and disorienting for nearly a minute. A spoken turn and a grunt of pain follow that passage, before the folky singing returns and the sequence begins again. These changes give the performance an unstable emotional temperature, passing from languor through confusion to an abrupt expression of hurt. The title also echoes the question about being an artist raised in her accompanying statement, which criticizes the glamour and hypocrisy she associates with the music industry. More of the room is audible on “Blood Everywhere.” Ambient tone surrounds deliberate guitar strumming and a simple melody, while Dizzy’s vocals remain eerily hushed and murmured. Rattling sounds enter later, introducing small disturbances around the subdued performance. With so much space audible around the guitar and voice, those noises become unusually noticeable. The song’s unease rests in that exposed setting, where a quiet rattle can feel as consequential as a raised voice. A dog barks at the opening of “Life Is A Dog,” before gentle guitar strumming accompanies bluesy, folky singing. Her lamenting delivery carries a deep sorrow, with eerie layers of reverberant vocals gathering around it. Midway through, the song pauses for a spectral vocal passage, distorted and unstable like a voice breaking up on the radio or a cassette warbling as it plays. The interruption is chilling, briefly displacing the familiar intimacy of guitar and singer. When the earlier strumming and vocal style resume, that sorrow remains central. In her release notes, Dizzy links the song to anger toward the world and the suffering she has endured; the lament in her delivery gives those stated concerns an aching musical form. The EP takes its name from that closing song’s premise: life is a dog, and the cake is a piece of herself offered in response. Across the record, the guitar’s simplicity leaves room for a remarkably changeable voice, capable of moving from a folky murmur to bluesy complaint, sensual ease, or something suddenly strange and difficult to place. Her most unsettling passages grow from alterations to that intimate relationship, making the return of a familiar vocal tone feel newly significant. Dizzy makes her preference clear: “I love amateur art. It’s the most beautiful.” Her defense of instinctive expression runs alongside a wish to reach other people living with depression, a purpose she explains in the release statement. That desire for connection gives a generous dimension to her forceful insistence on doing things her own way: “Whether you believe in me or not, I don’t care. Because I believe in myself and my guitar. Fuck the rest.” Doggy’s Cake is out now digitally, with vinyl and CD editions available through ElasticStage. Order the EP here. items.body: Review by tszirmay — By sheer perseverance and absolute luck , I landed on an online video of a piece from their previous debut album, recently released in September 2025. It was so good, I immediately purchased it on Bandcamp, as well as this November 2025 one. Why, may you ask? A multitude of conspirators united in getting me hooked on this new trouvaille, starting with the country of origin Poland, being an absolute well of incredible music in the past 40 years and still going strong. Secondly, my tastes have evolved very much into a definite zone of admiration for expressive bass guitar lines, faithfully adorned with terrific e-piano, organ and synths that come straight out of the instrumental jazz-rock, groove-fusion era of the late 60s and 70s (think Brian Auger, Booker T and the MGs and such) , all propulsed by a robustly-appointed beat factory. The energy is palpable, the passion overtly addictive and the mood positive and buoyant. If you are looking for depressive sonic compliance, listen away in another direction. The band is a trio (yup, no guitars) that favours a jumpy, organic, raw and yet plush style that could easily define the modern electro-jazz-disco-funk hybrid jam that one could enjoy with acts like Tobor Experiment, Bottazz!, London Underground, Project Gemini and surely many others yet to discover. Mind music one can dance to, tap fingers or feet uncontrollably and just smile along for the ride. Keyboardist extraordinaire Roman Wrobleski , bassist Orz and immaculate drummer Jacek Rezner combine to create real palpitating pieces that ooze class, sweat and brawn all in one groove.One can easily snap their fingers to the cool Pacific Coast luxuriance on "California Plum Color", a perfect introduction to their suave style, as described above, emitting a vintage vibe, not too far removed from those Ocean Eleven etc.. soundtracks. What makes this so compelling is the occasional twist in alterations, boldly inserting pools of effects and creative deflection to the highly melodic foundation. Roman's fingers dance over the ivories with skill and inspiration yet rigidly protecting the rhythm divine groove at all times.The similarly sized "Gradient 1" and "Gradient 2" for a one-two punch showcases the smoothness of tone and color, occasional swerves into hypnotic repetition that surely provides for bodily reactions to take place. Rezner's manic drumming sits well with the plump bass lines that cast the needed spell. The buzzing cymbal work in particular is noteworthy, a sizzling shuffle that swats indifference away like flies, urging, pushing and leaning on the pulse courageously throughout. The sparkling e-piano not only offers melody but also a high energy percussive slant that keeps the juices flowing, like layers of sonic terraces one after the other.The trio really keeps the pot boiling on the frothy "Antelope Color", the focus openly targeting the synthesized electronics as they become overtly experimental in the background, Rezner pounding hard and fast, Wroblewski whipping out a leaping organ rant and the bass keeping it all neat and orderly in between. Fascinating ! "Summer End Color" was leaving a hot and sweaty realm, gently blowing into a cooler expanse, as if frigid Arctic squalls intended to relieve the heat. The warm speed slowly winds down to a reverential ending.The highlight is revealed on the tow final pieces the "Oolong Color" clocking in at 4:39 and its extended 7:45 version, a dozen minutes of exuberant and expressive fusion of a substantial variety of stylistic categories that also includes ambient seagull screeches, a funk-jazz rhythmic palisade, and some grove-induces aural hallucinations, especially evident in the extended version, where there are some slight Ozric Tentacles sonorities (if one omits the psychedelic Ed Wynne guitar pirouettes) that keep the dreams alive. items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — The World of Genius Hans is an excellent example of the more jazz-oriented, experimental and eccentric side of early-70s progressive rock. The second album by the French band Moving Gelatine Plates, it dives deeply into the Canterbury Scene, combining progressive rock, jazz-rock, psychedelia and a good dose of satirical humor.What stands out the most is the complexity of the compositions. The songs seem carefully constructed, especially in their instrumental sections, featuring several rhythmic changes, thematic development and interesting interactions between the instruments. Despite this complexity, the changes generally feel natural and do not seem to exist merely to show off technical skills.The instrumentation is probably one of the album's greatest strengths. Guitars, bass, drums, keyboards, saxophones, flute and other instruments create a very rich sound. The musicians demonstrate good technical ability, but fortunately the virtuosity remains subordinate to the compositions. The result is a technically sophisticated album without becoming excessively cold or purely focused on instrumental showmanship.The influence of the Canterbury Scene is quite evident, especially from bands such as Caravan and Soft Machine. Some elements also recall the more eclectic and experimental side of progressive rock. Nevertheless, Moving Gelatine Plates manages to develop a personality of its own, particularly through its humor, unusual instrumentation and combination of jazz and progressive rock structures.The title track, "The World of Genius Hans," is the main highlight. At around 14 minutes, it features numerous rhythmic changes, strong jazz influences and interesting synthesizer passages. It summarizes the album's overall concept very well and demonstrates the band's ability to work with long compositions without abandoning melodic ideas."Funny Doll" and "Astromonster" are also among the best moments of the album. The former presents a very characteristic approach from the band, while "Astromonster" explores a more psychedelic and experimental atmosphere.Another positive aspect is the album's cohesion. Despite the variety of ideas and styles, the album works very well as a complete listening experience. There is a relatively consistent musical identity throughout the record, and the alternation between more intense, jazzy, psychedelic and humorous moments keeps the listener interested.The production also deserves praise. Even though this is an early-70s recording, the instruments are relatively easy to distinguish, allowing the listener to appreciate the details of the complex arrangements.I would not consider the album perfect. Although the compositions are very interesting, a few passages can feel somewhat random, and the influence of other Canterbury Scene bands is quite noticeable. Therefore, despite its quality and complexity, I would not place it among the absolutely essential progressive rock albums.Nevertheless, The World of Genius Hans is highly recommended for fans of the Canterbury Scene, jazz-rock and the more experimental sides of progressive rock. It should also appeal to jazz-fusion fans who are interested in exploring progressive rock.Best tracks:1. The World of Genius Hans2. Funny Doll3. AstromonsterHonorable mention: Les �tres d'Or (bonus track)A highly recommended album for fans of Canterbury Scene, jazz-rock and progressive rock, particularly for listeners who enjoy complex arrangements, unusual instrumentation, frequent rhythmic changes and a humorous experimental approach.

items.body: Los Angeles industrial/EBM act Frontal Boundary released “Alone EP” on 11 September 2026 through Alfa Matrix. The 8-track digital EP opens the door to the band’s forthcoming album “Shattered Mind”. The tracklist runs “Alone”, a cover of Garbage’s “Milk” featuring Kimber Parrish, an alternate version of “Alone”, and five remixes of the title track: by Assemblage 23, Protokoll 19, Reaper, Asphodel Ivory and The Axiom Divide. Alone EP by Frontal Boundary The title track explores isolation and grief, moving Frontal Boundary’s established dark electro toward more melodic, emotionally exposed songwriting. The five remixers each take “Alone” in a different direction, from Assemblage 23‘s atmospheric treatment to the harder electronic versions from Protokoll 19 and Reaper and the more experimental readings by Asphodel Ivory and The Axiom Divide. Frontal Boundary’s run on Alfa Matrix “Alone EP” follows a string of Alfa Matrix releases from the band. Frontal Boundary signed to the label in July 2025 with the “Hate” EP, followed by the 8-track “Faith” EP in September 2025 and the full-length album “Failure” on 12 December 2025, released as a digital edition and a limited 2CD set. The band closed out the “Failure” cycle with the 7-track “Burn” EP, featuring a cover of Filter’s “Hey Man Nice Shot”, on 24 April 2026. “Alone EP” is the band’s first release of the “Shattered Mind” era. About Frontal Boundary Frontal Boundary is a Los Angeles-based industrial/EBM project formed by Brendin Ross (ex-Bile, Dawn Of Ashes, Bornless Fire) in 2008. The project issued the demo “Never Ending” and the debut track “Mindfuck” in 2009, then released its first album, “Electronic Warfare”, on 6 January 2012, followed by a 2013 re-release as “Electronic Warfare V.2”. Ross toured the project alongside acts including God Module and Suicide Commando during this period. Vocalist Krz Souls (Dawn Of Ashes, Bornless Fire) joined in 2019, and the pair released the album “The Fall” on 19 March 2021. Synth player Jaysen Craves (Livernois) joined as a full member in 2023, the year Frontal Boundary signed to Re:Mission Entertainment. That signing led to the singles “Shutting Down” and “Without A Chance” and the album “Shutting Down” on 27 September 2024, followed by the remix collection “Shutting Down Remixed” in April 2025 and the “Hollow” EP with Unter Null in March 2025. Frontal Boundary moved to Alfa Matrix in 2025, releasing “Hate”, “Faith” and the album “Failure” before the “Burn” EP in April 2026. “Alone EP” continues that run and leads into the band’s fifth full-length album, “Shattered Mind”.

items.body: There exists a certain species of electronic music that has been embalmed by its own admirers, preserved beneath enough black clothing, antique drum machines, and solemn references to 1981 that you half expect the Smithsonian to issue the next twelve-inch. Mercury Girl’s latest single Spirit Forward escapes that mausoleum because Aaron Pena sounds less interested in curating the past than in using its machinery to pick a fight with the present. Pena, the Filipino American San Diego musician behind Mercury Girl, works with the familiar furniture of cold wave: stiff percussion, bass lines that keep walking even when the room feels empty, synthesizers that seem permanently one bad voltage spike away from collapse. Spirit Forward, however, has a wiry nervous energy that puts it somewhere between Black Marble’s private unease, the laboratory pop of Oppenheimer Analysis, Tom Vek’s angular minimalism, and the sideways rhythmic intelligence of Talking Heads. The bass carries most of the physical argument, a rubbery little engine repeating itself beneath chords that keep looking upward as though expecting an answer from a ceiling full of dead fluorescent tubes. The question is the oldest one available: “What’s the meaning of all of this?” Pena understands that asking it in 2026 means pushing through advertising, algorithms, compulsory self-branding, endless feeds, and the faint suspicion that somebody has already converted your existential crisis into a subscription tier. Its beat suggests motion without destination, which turns out to be a useful musical equivalent for living inside a culture forever promising connection while quietly perfecting isolation. “This song mirrors the frustrations I, and I’m sure many others, have had when trying to make sense of life and the meaning behind it, especially in a world so enveloped with distracting you from doing so,” says Pena. “We’re all fed ideas about who and what we should be; this song rejects those expectations.” Pena recorded the material with vintage synthesizers and half-working sequencers, and you can hear the appeal of equipment that misbehaves, because human uncertainty sounds better when the machines possess a little uncertainty of their own. The arrangement has space, but never comfort; every open patch seems to leave another philosophical bill unpaid. Listen to Spirit Forward below and order the single here. Spirit Forward by Mercury Girl Ahead of Mercury Girl’s debut album, A NuTone, Spirit Forward makes a persuasive case for Pena as a songwriter who understands that cold wave can still carry blood, doubt, humour, and the embarrassing human need to ask enormous questions while the drum machine keeps perfect time. ロン・カーター×ヨタム・シルバースタイン、ピアノレス・デュオの系譜 ジャズ専門誌『Jazz Journal』が8-9月の新譜ガイドを発表した。中でも注目したいのが、ベーシスト、ロン・カーターとギタリスト、ヨタム・シルバースタインによるデュエット作である。これはジム・ホールへのトリビュートとして企画されたという。   ロン・カーターとジム・ホールは、かつてベースとギターだけで対話する録音を残している。伴奏を必要としないピアノレス・デュオという形式は、当時としては実験的な試みだった。今回のシルバースタインとの再演は、その系譜を半世紀後の若い世代の手に橋渡しする作業とも言える。 なお同時期には、Sidiki Camaraの野心作、Tristan Cappelの追悼盤、15年ぶりとなるDeirdre インタビューでハリソンは、サンダースの音の探求とサン・ラーの宇宙的な音楽哲学、二人の巨人がそれぞれ異なる方向からスピリチュアル・ジャズの地平を切り開いていった様子を語る。一人の証人が二つの潮流を同時に見ていたという事実は、ジャズ史を線ではなく面として捉え直す手がかりになる。デトロイトという土地が、ニューヨークとは異なる形でアヴァンギャルドの拠点になり得たことも、この証言を通じて浮かび上がってくる。 On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the major players of the 21st century folk revival scene, JOANNA NEWSOM has foundinternational fame with her unique musical performances that includes intricate harp instrumentationand a very unusual quirky vocal style. While her album "Ys" would propel to folk royalty, her debutrelease THE MILK-EYED MENDER was met with positive critique and universal love as well. NEWSOM grewup in Grass Valley, California and is actually distantly related to the state's governor. NEWSOM wasgifted with a rather quick ascent to fame after only appearing as a guest musician on a Nervous Copalbum before setting out on her own and capturing the folk world's attention in record time. After acouple warmup EPs, she has released four critically acclaimed albums so far.THE MILK-EYED MENDER was NEWSOM's debut which not only showcased her multi-instrumental talents thatincluded harpsichord, piano, keyboards and harp but also featured her unique songwriting styles thathad one foot in the catchy world of pop music while maintaining an authentic medieval feel detachedfrom the modern day excesses of production and technology overload. This is a solo album frombeginning to end with NEWSOM performing every instrumental and having written and sung every song.While "Ys" would evolve NEWSOM's sound into a more complex orchestral production, THE MILK-EYEDMENDER is the perfect place to inure your musical sensibilities to NEWSOM's bizarre sounding vocalidiosyncrasies.The album features 12 tracks that add up to just over 52 minutes and all written by NEWSOM herselfexcept the traditional folk song "Three Little Babies." The album indeed comes off as a collectionof child-like songs structured around the harp which plays an interesting role as both the basis forrhythm as well as providing the melodic backing to NEWSOM's lyrical performances. The album alsofeatures both acoustic and electric pianos as well as harpsichord but the album is fairly sparse asfar as instrumentation and showcases NEWSOM's ability to express herself through the barest of bonessimplicity and yet sounding somehow uncannily complete with the harp alone serving as the entireinstrumentation for the majority of the album's run.While the most stripped down and most accessible of NEWSOM's releases that would become moreexperimental after this one's release, THE MILK-EYED MENDER holds up as a well-constructed piece ofharp-based folk music in its own right despite no excursions into the progressive chamber folk thatwould find her embraced by the modern New Weird America culture that found NEWSOM in the company ofthe likes of Devendra Barnhart, Animal Collective and Espers. Ironically this strong debut wouldprove to only be the beginning for NEWSOM who quickly captured the momentum and expanded herambitions into the world of more complex progressive arenas. Many may find this a bit too naive andinnocent in comparison to the grandiosity of "Ys" however it's exactly the bare bones authenticitythat i find appealing about this debut which establishes NEWSOM as a talent in her own right beforegoing into more adventurous collaborative efforts.

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — 'The Piper At the Gates of Dawn' is the 1967 debut album by British rock band Pink Floyd. I always thought I was fine with experimental music, that I was open-minded enough to enjoy music that deviates from traditional songwriting practices. But perhaps I was wrong, because this album is completely and utterly "out there", and my delicate senses just can't cope. Somehow, Pink Floyd went from this album to eventually becoming one of the biggest bands in history, but I've yet to figure out how. I give them credit for completely throwing out the rulebook and thinking outside the box, but that doesn't necessarily mean these songs are actually any good. Because I find them boring as hell. The only one that remotely stands out to me, is 'The Gnome', but there's no way I'm going out of my way to listen to it. These might have been revolutionary and exciting back in the 1960's, but that's way ahead of my time, and by today's standards, I'll be having none of this. Still, regardless of this debut, Pink Floyd really are one of the biggest bands of all time, so I'll continue on my personal Floyd journey, and will see what their next album has in store for me.

items.body: Ultravox released their fifth studio album, “Rage in Eden,” on 11 September 1981 through Chrysalis Records. The British new wave band recorded the nine-track album with producer Conny Plank at his studio near Cologne, West Germany, following the commercial breakthrough of “Vienna” a year earlier. “Rage in Eden” turns 45 this year. Where the “Vienna” sessions had been rehearsed live before the band entered the studio, Ultravox spent three months making “Rage in Eden,” building songs directly out of studio experiments; the title track grew from a backwards playback of vocals recorded for “I Remember (Death in the Afternoon).” The album runs 45 minutes and 34 seconds across nine tracks: “The Voice,” “We Stand Alone,” “Rage in Eden,” “I Remember (Death in the Afternoon),” “The Thin Wall,” “Stranger Within,” “Accent on Youth,” “The Ascent” and “Your Name (Has Slipped My Mind Again),” with the final three forming a continuous sequence on side two. Warren Cann (drums, electronic percussion, vocals), Chris Cross (bass, synthesizers, vocals), Billy Currie (synthesizers, piano, violin, viola) and Midge Ure (lead vocals, guitars, synthesizers) wrote and performed every song, with the original sleeve designed by Peter Saville Associates. Two singles from the album, “The Thin Wall” and “The Voice,” reached number 14 and number 16 on the UK singles chart, while the album itself peaked at number 4 and was certified Gold by the BPI. “Rage in Eden” streams on Spotify. About Ultravox Ultravox formed in London in April 1974 as Tiger Lily, led by Royal College of Art student Dennis Leigh, later known as John Foxx, alongside Chris Allen, later Chris Cross, on bass and Stevie Shears on guitar, joined that year by drummer Warren Cann and violinist Billy Currie. After several name changes the band signed to Island Records in 1976 and settled on Ultravox!, with the exclamation mark a reference to the krautrock band Neu!, while finishing its 1977 debut, “Ultravox!,” produced by Steve Lillywhite and Brian Eno. “Ha! Ha! Ha!” followed later that year, and 1978’s “Systems of Romance,” produced by Conny Plank, brought synthesizers to the front of the band’s sound. Island dropped Ultravox at the end of 1978, and John Foxx left in March 1979 to pursue a solo career. Midge Ure, previously of Slik and the Rich Kids and a touring member of Thin Lizzy, joined as vocalist, guitarist and keyboardist after collaborating with Billy Currie in the studio project Visage. The reshaped band signed to Chrysalis Records, and “Vienna,” released in July 1980 and again produced by Conny Plank, gave Ultravox its commercial breakthrough: the title single reached number 2 on the UK chart in January 1981. “Rage in Eden” followed on 11 September 1981, again recorded with Plank at his Cologne studio, reaching number 4 in the UK and earning a Gold certification from the BPI. Ultravox then worked with producer George Martin on 1982’s “Quartet,” which reached number 6 in the UK and produced four Top 20 singles, before self-producing 1984’s “Lament,” which included the UK number 3 hit “Dancing with Tears in My Eyes.” That November, Midge Ure co-wrote and produced Band Aid’s “Do They Know It’s Christmas?,” and Ultravox performed at Live Aid in 1985. Warren Cann left the band in 1986, and “U-Vox,” recorded with Big Country’s Mark Brzezicki on drums, became the final album of the original run before Ultravox split in 1987. Billy Currie led a new line-up through two further albums, “Revelation” (1993) and “Ingenuity” (1994), before the band dissolved again in 1996. The classic line-up of Cann, Cross, Currie and Ure reformed in 2008 for the “Return to Eden” tour and released the studio album “Brilliant” in May 2012, followed by a run of UK arena dates with Simple Minds that closed with a show at the O2 Arena in November 2013. Bassist Chris Cross died in March 2024, as Side-Line reported at the time. In October 2025, Chrysalis continued the catalogue’s reissue campaign with “The Collection (Deluxe Edition),” gathering the band’s 1980s singles. “Rage in Eden,” the fifth studio album that captured Ultravox at its most exploratory in the Cologne studio, turns 45 this year.
items._cn_summary: 这是关于Ultravox第五张录音室专辑《Rage in Eden》发行45周年的纪念性新闻稿。专辑于1981年由Chrysalis Records发行，由德国制作人Conny Plank在科隆附近的录音室制作，历时三个月完成。与前作《Vienna》预先现场排练的录制方式不同，本作的九首曲目完全从录音室实验中生发而成，标题曲即源于对另一首歌曲人声的逆向播放处理。专辑在英国榜达到第四位并获BPI金唱片认证，其中单曲《The Thin Wall》和《The Voice》分别进入前二十。文章同时回顾了乐队从1974年组建以来的历史脉络，从早期的实验性电子倾向到Midge Ure加入后转向主流新流行的过程。整篇文章以事实性介绍为主，缺乏深度乐评分析。

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body: Light percussion opens “Down Home”, the new single from Melbourne instrumental funk quartet Karate Boogaloo, before a bass line takes the lead at an easy mid-tempo. The drums lock into a hard, tight pocket on a kit that sounds close to falling apart, while organ and choppy guitar come in over the top. That rattling kit gives the rough edge to a tune named after anything simple and worn in. The main theme leans openly on nostalgia, and the band reckon anyone who has declared the riff dead should “check their specs“. Drummer Hudson Whitlock plays alongside Henry Jenkins on bass, Callum Riley on organ and Darvid Thor on guitar. The four met as classmates at a Melbourne high school and have played together for almost two decades. In our July interview with the band, Jenkins explained that Karate Boogaloo began strictly as a covers act devoted to The Meters and Booker T. & The MG’s. The change came with an original called “Stay Healthy”, which he described as the moment the band “crossed the River Rubicon“. “Down Home” precedes Access All Areas, due on 9 October through Colemine Records and College of Knowledge Records. In February 2027 Karate Boogaloo tour the UK, France and the Netherlands. The run opens on 3 February aboard V11, a 1951 British lightship docked in Rotterdam, and closes upstairs at Paradiso in Amsterdam on the 13th. The London date is at the Jazz Cafe on 5 February. Further nights follow at Hyde Park Book Club in Leeds, The Abbey in Manchester, The Jam Jar in Bristol, Le Tetris in Le Havre and POPUP! in Paris.
